draft.body:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

writer_sources.snapshot: This fictional memo compares two observation weeks. There were 160 boardings in week A and 240 boardings in week B. Boardings count trips, not unique people. No attendance data were collected. The weeks differed in academic schedule, and the pilot was not randomized. The memo does not estimate the effect of the shuttle on attendance.

writer_sources.title: Synthetic rider survey methods note
writer_sources.snapshot: Eighteen voluntary survey responses were collected from shuttle riders. Fourteen respondents said they valued later service. Non-riders were not surveyed. The responses describe these respondents and cannot establish demand across all students. No cost or emissions measurements were collected.
